title: Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds
text:
1 Project Overview
This book documents the reproducible workflow for a global comparative analysis of environmental variation and extra-pair paternity (EPP) in birds.
The project focuses on annual, population-level estimates of EPP in socially monogamous bird species. Each record represents a population-level estimate of the proportion of broods containing at least one extra-pair young in a defined study year or study period, linked to geographic coordinates, breeding-season timing, environmental variables, and phylogenetic information.

text:
1.1 Scope of the Dataset
The analysis is restricted to records that meet the criteria below. These rules keep the dataset comparable across species, populations, and study systems.






ImportantInclusion Criteria




The species is classified as socially monogamous.
The EPP estimate is available for a known year or study period.
The number of sampled broods and the number of broods with EPP are known.
Geographic coordinates are available or can be assigned reliably.
The breeding season can be linked to monthly environmental data.
The species can be matched to the taxonomic and phylogenetic backbone used in the analysis.

1.2 Predictor Groups
Environmental predictors are organized into four broad groups.


1.2.1 Mean Climatic Conditions
Seasonal or monthly temperature and precipitation values linked to each EPP record.


1.2.2 Climatic Variability
Measures such as diurnal temperature range or within-season variation in temperature and precipitation.


1.2.3 Environmental Anomalies
Short-term and long-term deviations from local climatic baselines.


1.2.4 Habitat Productivity
NDVI-based measures of vegetation productivity during the relevant breeding-season window.

title: Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds
text:
1.4 Workflow
The book is organized as a reproducible research workflow, moving from raw data preparation to analytical outputs.


Data preparation - cleaning the raw EPP dataset and checking response variables, breeding-system categories, coordinates, dates, and sampling effort.
Taxonomic matching and phylogeny - matching species names to the taxonomic backbone and preparing the phylogenetic covariance matrix.
Environmental variables - linking each EPP record to climate and NDVI data using location, year, and breeding-season timing.
Exploratory analyses - summarising sample sizes, missing data, predictor distributions, and correlations among environmental variables.
Overall model diagnostics - evaluating the random-effect structure used in the EPP models.
Environmental models - fitting beta-binomial models of EPP while accounting for population, species, and phylogenetic non-independence.
Figures - producing model summaries, posterior predictions, and manuscript-ready figures.

text:
1.5 Key Terms

Extra-pair paternity (EPP)
The occurrence of offspring within a socially monogamous brood that are sired by a male other than the social father.
Population-level estimate
An EPP estimate associated with a particular population, study site, year, or study period.
Environmental anomaly
A deviation in environmental conditions from a relevant long-term baseline.







CautionReproducibility Principle



Every analytical decision should be traceable from raw input data to final figures, tables, and model outputs.

3 Aim
This page documents the provenance of the environmental variables used in the EPP analyses. The goal is to make clear which variables are included in the final public dataset, which external data products were used, and which extraction scripts are provided in the GitHub repository.






NoteRepository Principle



The repository contains the final analysis-ready dataset, metadata, model code, and lightweight extraction scripts where possible. Large external climate and remote-sensing products are documented but not redistributed.




4 Final analysis dataset
The final dataset used in the analyses is:
epp_data_June2026.csv
Variable definitions are provided in:
metadata_June2026.csv
These files contain the EPP records, taxonomy, geographic information, breeding-season timing, environmental variables, and derived covariates used by the models.

6 CRU climate variables
Monthly climate variables were derived from external CRU climate data before being merged into the final EPP dataset. The raw CRU files are not included in the GitHub repository because they are external data products and may be large, versioned, or subject to their own distribution terms.
The final dataset includes the derived climate variables needed for the analyses:

first-month and full-season mean temperature;
first-month and full-season precipitation;
first-month and full-season diurnal temperature range;
short-term 5-year temperature and precipitation anomalies;
long-term 1961-1989 temperature and precipitation anomalies.







ImportantClimate Reproducibility



The published analyses can be rerun from epp_data_June2026.csv without downloading the raw CRU files. Full re-extraction of the climate variables would require access to the same external CRU data and the local extraction workflow used to generate the derived variables.




7 NDVI extraction
NDVI was used as a proxy for habitat productivity around each study location. The final variables describe median NDVI within a 30 km buffer around the EPP study coordinates for the first breeding-season month and, where relevant, the full breeding season.
The NDVI values were extracted using Google Earth Engine. The JavaScript script used for the NDVI extraction is provided in the GitHub repository with the environmental extraction scripts.
The final NDVI variables included in epp_data_June2026.csv are:

ndvi_first_month_median_30km;
ndvi_full_season_median_30km;
ndvi_start_month;
ndvi_end_month;
ndvi_year;
ndvi_merge_status.



8 Daily weather variability
Daily weather variability was extracted from ERA5-Land using Google Earth Engine for the first breeding-season month. These variables were used to quantify short-term weather variability during the period most directly linked to breeding.
The Earth Engine export merged into the final dataset is stored as:
data/processed/epp_era5_land_daily_variability_first_month.csv
The extracted daily-weather summaries include:

daily temperature mean, range, and standard deviation;
daily precipitation mean, maximum, total, and standard deviation;
number of wet days with precipitation greater than 1 mm.

The corresponding Google Earth Engine JavaScript extraction script is provided in the repository.


9 Taxonomy
Family-level taxonomy was added from the Clements Checklist v2025 using the matched Clements_name field. This step produced the family and order variables used in the family-level descriptive and sensitivity analyses.
The Clements checklist file used for the merge is:
data_raw/Clements_v2025-October-2025.csv
The helper script for the family merge is:
scripts/add_clements_family.py


10 What Is Needed to Reproduce the Analyses
To reproduce the models reported in this project, a user needs:

epp_data_June2026.csv;
metadata_June2026.csv;
data/processed/dat_model_phylo.rds;
data/processed/phylo_mat.rds;
the Quarto files documenting the workflow.

To reproduce the environmental extraction from raw source products, a user would additionally need access to the CRU climate files and the cloud-hosted Google Earth Engine products used for NDVI and ERA5-Land daily weather.






TipPublication Strategy



For GitHub publication, the repository provides the final analysis-ready data, metadata, extraction scripts where possible, and clear provenance.

title: 4  Taxonomy and phylogeny
text:
5 Aim
This page prepares the taxonomic and phylogenetic structure used in the Bayesian comparative analyses.
The goal is to verify species matching between the analytical dataset and the phylogenetic tree, prune the tree to the species included in the study, generate a phylogenetic correlation matrix, and prepare the phylogenetic grouping variables required for the Bayesian models.


6 Load packages and data


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(ape)
library(knitr)

dat_model <- readRDS("data/processed/dat_model.rds")

dat_taxonomy <- readr::read_csv(
  "epp_data_June2026.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  select(
    any_of(
      c(
        "epp_row_id",
        "record_id",
        "scientific_name",
        "Clements_name",
        "order",
        "family",
        "family_common"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct()

if (
  !"family" %in% names(dat_model) ||
    ("family" %in% names(dat_model) && all(is.na(dat_model$family)))
) {
  dat_model <- dat_model %>%
    select(-any_of(c("order", "family", "family_common")))
}

needs_family_merge <- !"family" %in% names(dat_model) ||
  all(is.na(dat_model$family))

if (needs_family_merge && "epp_row_id" %in% names(dat_model)) {
  dat_model <- dat_model %>%
    left_join(
      dat_taxonomy %>%
        select(
          epp_row_id,
          any_of(c("order", "family", "family_common"))
        ),
      by = "epp_row_id"
    )
}

needs_family_merge <- !"family" %in% names(dat_model) ||
  all(is.na(dat_model$family))

if (needs_family_merge && "record_id" %in% names(dat_model)) {
  dat_model <- dat_model %>%
    left_join(
      dat_taxonomy %>%
        select(
          record_id,
          any_of(c("order", "family", "family_common"))
        ),
      by = "record_id"
    )
}

needs_family_merge <- !"family" %in% names(dat_model) ||
  all(is.na(dat_model$family))

if (needs_family_merge && "Clements_name" %in% names(dat_model)) {
  dat_model <- dat_model %>%
    left_join(
      dat_taxonomy %>%
        select(
          Clements_name,
          any_of(c("order", "family", "family_common"))
        ) %>%
        distinct(),
      by = "Clements_name"

12 Prepare phylogenetic grouping variables
Two species-level grouping variables were retained for the Bayesian models:

species_phylo - species identity linked to the phylogenetic covariance matrix;
species_nonphylo - species identity modelled as an additional non-phylogenetic random effect.

Including both random effects allows the models to partition variation attributable to shared evolutionary history and species-specific variation not explained by phylogeny.

  mutate(
    species_phylo = Clements_name,
    species_nonphylo = scientific_name

  filter(
    species_phylo %in% tree_pruned$tip.label
  )

title: 5  Selection of the random-effect structure
text:
6 Aim
This page evaluates the random-effect structure used in the Bayesian phylogenetic models.
The primary goal is to determine whether study identity should be retained in addition to population identity. Because multiple observations may originate from the same population and some populations may be represented in multiple studies, these grouping factors can partially overlap.
To assess the importance of study identity, we first quantify the overlap between populations and studies and then compare two alternative random-effect structures:

Population identity only.
Population identity plus study identity.

Both models additionally account for species-level variation and phylogenetic relatedness among species.


7 Load packages and data


Show code
library(brms)
library(loo)
library(knitr)
library(tidyverse)

dat_model_phylo <- readRDS("data/processed/dat_model_phylo.rds")
phylo_mat <- readRDS("data/processed/phylo_mat.rds")




8 Prepare model dataset


Show code
dat_basic_phylo <- dat_model_phylo

Because most variation occurred among species, we also explored whether avian families differed in the extent of among-species divergence in EPP.

if ("family" %in% names(dat_var) && any(!is.na(dat_var$family))) {
  species_family_epp <- dat_var %>%
    filter(
      !is.na(family),
      !is.na(species_phylo)

    group_by(family, species_phylo) %>%
    summarise(
      species_mean_epp = weighted_mean(epp_rate, n_broods_sampled),
      total_broods = sum(n_broods_sampled, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_records = n(),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  family_species_variation <- species_family_epp %>%
    group_by(family) %>%
    summarise(
      n_species = n_distinct(species_phylo),
      mean_species_epp = mean(species_mean_epp, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_species_epp = sd(species_mean_epp, na.rm = TRUE),
      min_species_epp = min(species_mean_epp, na.rm = TRUE),
      max_species_epp = max(species_mean_epp, na.rm = TRUE),
      range_species_epp = max_species_epp - min_species_epp,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    filter(n_species >= 3) %>%
    arrange(desc(sd_species_epp))

  family_mean_scale_correlation <- cor.test(
    family_species_variation$mean_species_epp,
    family_species_variation$sd_species_epp,
    method = "pearson"
  )

  family_mean_scale_model <- lm(
    sd_species_epp ~ mean_species_epp,
    data = family_species_variation
  )

  family_mean_scale_summary <- data.frame(
    statistic = c(
      "Pearson correlation",
      "Correlation p-value",
      "Linear-model R-squared"
    ),
    value = c(
      unname(family_mean_scale_correlation$estimate),
      family_mean_scale_correlation$p.value,
      summary(family_mean_scale_model)$r.squared
    )
  )

  kable(family_species_variation, digits = 3)

9 Aim
The aim of this analysis is to test whether variation in extra-pair paternity (EPP) is associated with environmental conditions experienced during the breeding season.
To evaluate different environmental hypotheses, three Bayesian phylogenetic beta-binomial models were fitted:
All models additionally include a common set of geographic and methodological moderators:
These variables were included to account for broad geographic gradients and methodological differences among studies that may influence estimates of EPP.
All models further account for population-level variation, species identity, and phylogenetic relatedness among species through random effects.
Together, these models allow us to distinguish whether EPP is more strongly associated with absolute environmental conditions, short-term environmental fluctuations, or departures from long-term climatic expectations.
All continuous predictors are standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Absolute precipitation is log-transformed as log(x + 1) before standardisation to reduce skewness.

extract_fixed_effects <- function(model, model_label, term_labels) {
  draws <- as_draws_df(model)

  available_terms <- intersect(names(term_labels), names(draws))

  do.call(
    rbind,
    lapply(
      available_terms,
      function(term) {
        x <- draws[[term]]

        data.frame(
          model = model_label,
          term = term,
          predictor = term_labels[[term]],
          estimate = median(x),
          lower = quantile(x, 0.025),
          upper = quantile(x, 0.975),
          prob_positive = mean(x > 0),
          prob_negative = mean(x < 0),
          row.names = NULL
        )
      }
    )
  )
}
